newsitem.title: POLAND: Germany's Herzog in Gdansk talks of healing wounds.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Herzog in Gdansk talks of healing wounds.

text.p: German President Roman Herzog, visiting Poland's city of Gdansk from which Germans were expelled after World War Two, said past wounds had not all healed but both nations were working hard to cure them.

Herzog recalled that Gdansk was rebuilt from its wartime ruins partly by Poles expelled from the country's eastern lands which had been lost to the then Soviet Union, while the city's German residents had been forced to start again in the West.
"All this left deep wounds," Herzog said in a speech at a ceremony linked with the Baltic city's millenium this year.
"Not all of them have healed already, although Germans and Poles are doing much to ensure shadows of the past fade in the new century and will not burden young generations," he said.
Gdansk, formerly Danzig, was the site of Nazi Germany's first onslaught on Poland in 1939 at the start of the war.
Gdansk's Jews were murdered by the Nazis and its German population was then expelled by communist authorities at the end of the war when Poland's borders were shifted westwards.

Starting his visit to Gdansk, accompanied by Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski, Herzog laid a wreath at the wartime Polish military outpost of Westerplatte which was shelled during the Nazi assault on the then free city.
Earlier the presidents opened an art exhibition in Warsaw recalling the era when Poland and Saxony shared common kings.

Germany is now the strongest champion of Polish aspirations to NATO and the European Union as well as its main trading partner and the two countries are striving to make popular feelings catch up with political and economic developments.
Herzog has played a key role in this process, including his apology, on the 50th anniversary of the 1944 Warsaw Uprising, for the suffering Nazi Germany caused Poland in World War Two.
Herzog applauded the fact that Poland was now free and could join European structures, saying: "For its German neighbours, it would be hard to find better news."
He recalled in his speech that Gdansk gave birth in 1980 to the Solidarity free trade union whose struggle against communist rule helped pave the way for German unification.
The ex-communist Kwasniewski also praised Solidarity's past role in his speech at the Gdansk ceremony, opening a gathering of the New Hansa, a grouping of more than 100 coastal cities.

"From here blew the wind which changed the face of Europe," said Kwasniewski, who is now a social democrat but who was the target of a protest by hundreds of his political opponents who are numerous in the Solidarity stronghold.
Herzog was later due to visit former Polish president and Solidarity founder Lech Walesa who lives there.
